extracted.intended_audience: advertising and marketing researchers and practitioners (academics, agency strategists, and graduate students)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological guidance for designing, executing, analyzing, and applying advertising and marketing research (consumer information-seeking, new product testing, social marketing, subjective/Q-methodology, and media-exposure studies). Emphasizes sampling, measurement, analytic techniques, and practical implications for advertisers and policymakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative sampling and recall window
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a national random sample (example: 1,300 households excluding Alaska) and focus on respondents who purchased within a defined recent period (example: purchases in the 13 months preceding interviews). Each interview focused on only one product purchase per household.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure sample representativeness and restrict recall to a bounded recent period to reduce recall bias; concentrate each interview on a single purchase episode to obtain detailed data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect product-specific background data
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect specific questions about the purchase (car or appliance), experience with the product category, individual's product purchase history, and household demographic categorizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine event-specific details with broader category experience and demographics so explanatory variables (experience, satisfaction, demographics) can be related to information-seeking behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use both aided and unaided recall techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Both aided and unaided recall questions were used regarding ranking of information sources as to their importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare results from aided vs unaided recall — the type of question used and the ranking criteria materially affect findings (e.g., advertising often ranks low in unaided recall but higher on other question types). Do not accept single-method rankings without checking alternative question formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure multiple information sources and complementary media roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers use more than one type of information source before buying; different media serve different and complementary roles in the consumer's search for information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design instruments to capture multiple sources and the distinct roles of different media rather than assuming a single dominant source; avoid treating advertising as the sole information provider.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate amount and timing of information seeking
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate how long buyers spend on the purchase decision (example finding: about half spend only a few weeks) and determine turnover of prospective purchasers actively seeking information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use timing measures to inform advertising timing and content strategy — adjust campaigns for rapid turnover; collect duration measures (decision time) and relate them to experience and satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model combined effects and interactions of explanatory variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that personal and product variables often do not adequately explain differences when considered singly; variables interact and their combined influence is crucial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate and test complex explanatory variables (e.g., 'life style') composed of interacting component variables; empirically determine which components interact and treat interacting groups as new predictors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multivariate/interaction-detecting analytic techniques (AID and MCA example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply sophisticated computer techniques (example: AID—Automatic Interaction Detector—and MCA—Multiple Classification Analysis—in tandem) to determine which variables, in combination, best distinguish individuals with different levels of information-seeking behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ methods that detect interactions and allow assessment of combined predictive power; use analysis to investigate interrelationship among explanatory variables and overall predictive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare types of analytic evidence and balance cost vs decision-utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Different decision-makers prefer different information types; expensive test-marketing data often confirm or refine decisions made on less costly data rather than serve as 'go/no-go' determinants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing evaluation, consider cost-effectiveness and the practical decision use of data: which data are used by managers to make initial vs confirmatory decisions?

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and use empirically validated respondent types ('predictors')
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of relying solely on 'heavy users' or 'new-product triers', identify respondents who have demonstrated past predictive accuracy ('predictors'), who predicted new product success more accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop criteria or screening methods to find respondents with predictive track records; these respondents can provide more efficient and valid forecasts of new product acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segment markets by promotion-effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Some individuals respond best to advertising while others are most influenced by product sampling, suggesting segmentation in terms of promotion-effectiveness criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test differential effectiveness of promotion tactics across segments and plan promotion mix accordingly rather than applying a uniform promotion strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentally test social-responsibility and integration effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental studies (example: racial prejudice and integrated advertising) showed differential audience reactions (e.g., prejudiced whites react adversely to ads featuring non-whites) with carry-over effects to products and sponsoring companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include audience attitudinal measures (such as prejudice) and measure potential carry-over effects on product/company image; weigh potential adverse reactions against broader benefits of integrated messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure self-concept dimensions and consider product conspicuousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis tested whether actual ('real') or aspired ('ideal') self-concept predicts brand preference, with a finding that actual self-concept was more predictive across conspicuous and inconspicuous products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include measures of both actual and ideal self-concept when assessing brand preference and tailor message strategy accordingly; do not assume ideal self will dominate for conspicuous products without testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate advertising types in organizational/industrial contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising is important in industrial purchasing; particular types of institutional advertisements can be more effective than product advertisements for little-known suppliers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating industrial advertising, distinguish institutional vs product ads and measure their relative effectiveness for supplier awareness and sales; consider advertising's role in raising awareness for lesser-known suppliers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Q-Methodology correctly for subjective-segmentation studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Q-Methodology: individuals sort statement cards into evaluative categories along an eleven-point scale with instructions to produce a 'quasi-normal' distribution and exact numbers per category; factor analysis groups individuals by similarity of responses to segment subjective viewpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Q-technique procedures: enforce distribution requirements, use intensive individual-level data (not mass-population sampling), and apply factor-analytic procedures to identify subjective groups. The goal is to segment by shared values/subjective orientations, not to measure group prevalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design field studies with demographic and contextual comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Field studies (example: Cleveland, Philadelphia, Lansing) compared media use and attitudes across blacks/whites, urban/suburban/rural, and adults/children, to understand channel access, attitudes, and content preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include multiple sites and demographic groups, and compare against general population samples where possible to identify distinct behavioral patterns and implications for targeting and message design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify media exposure and relate it to awareness/outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure television exposure (hours/day) and relate exposure to awareness of expert information sources; high TV use related to greater awareness but highest awareness among those with diverse interpersonal contacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect quantitative media-use measures and analyze their relation to outcome variables (awareness, knowledge); control for interpersonal contact diversity and social network breadth as moderators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirically test social marketing model transferability
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether knowledge from product marketing transfers to social marketing; conduct empirical studies and field experiments (example: a Costa Rica survey and model testing) to test social marketing models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume direct transferability—empirically test models in social contexts, include behavioral and psychosocial variables, and disseminate findings to practitioners and policymakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disseminate usable outputs for practitioners and educators
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques and research findings should constitute a basis for development of useful teaching materials and management development programs; research should inform marketing managers' information needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce publications, reports, and teaching materials translating research findings into actionable guidance for managers and agency strategists; emphasize applicability and decision-oriented insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mixed methods and compare question/measurement effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Because responses vary by question type and ranking criteria, compare different question formats and ranking criteria (e.g., aided vs unaided recall, multiple ranking methods) before accepting consumer judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design studies to include and compare multiple measurement methods; interpret differences as methodological artifacts rather than pure reflections of consumer cognition.
